messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Two decades earlier, Rajesh had been held captive for eleven days in a windowless storage container during a cross-border supply chain inspection. The kidnapping unfolded at precisely four o’clock in the afternoon, and as the sun dipped, his captors dragged thick, coiled ropes across the concrete floor, the hissing sound of the fibers against stone etching itself into his memory. He had been left alone in pitch blackness, waking only to the sound of boots pacing outside, and the ordeal lasted through the coldest nights of the year. When he finally escaped, the specific geometry of that capture—the exact hour, the coiled manacles, the suffocating dark—became the blueprint for his fear. Over the following months, those same cues began to dictate his daily reality. At the distribution center where Rajesh now worked as a warehouse worker, the loading bay doors began to slam shut at four in the afternoon, casting long, narrowing shadows across the asphalt. The sight of a coiled fire hose on the receiving dock, or even a photograph of a snake in a colleague’s photo album, instantly threw him on high alert. Because the familiar darkness of the warehouse aisles mirrored his imprisonment, his nervous system locked into a state of hypervigilance; he found it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, and his eyes constantly darted toward the rear doors as if he frequently looked behind him to check if someone was following him. When the afternoon light faded and the warehouse floor plunged into shadow, the memory of the unending dark overwhelmed him, compelling him to retreat to his truck during his night shift. He refused to go to sleep or lie in the dark, instead standing in the cab while he constantly checked his body for signs of danger or injury, patting down his arms and ribs for bruises that never appeared. Each time the industrial lights flickered, he would pull out his phone and call his wife, insisting, I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay. The exhaustion of this vigilance slowly fractured his sense of self. Because he could not stop his own scanning or demand constant external validation, he began to feel utterly powerless, convincing himself that he can't stop bad things from happening to me. This erosion of control bled into his worldview; he stopped seeking comfort inwardly because he believed that if I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, and instead projected his fragility outward. His refusal to rest and his constant reassurance seeking left him perpetually on edge, which meant that minor environmental cues began to feel as threatening as the ropes of his captivity. A neighbor’s garden hose unspooling on the pavement or the distant clatter of a delivery truck suddenly triggered the same panic, because his depleted state lowered his threshold for threat. Believing his continued existence was a burden, he stopped looking for safety and instead braced for catastrophe. I am not sure my life is worth living anymore became the quiet undercurrent of his days, and as he withdrew from his marriage and his shift schedules grew erratic, the negative appraisal cemented his perception of danger. The conviction that he was fundamentally helpless and that his life had lost its value directly fed his ongoing threat response, making the nighttime hours feel permanently unsafe and keeping his system locked in a perpetual state of watchfulness. The cycle tightened without his awareness: the triggers sparked the strategies, the strategies eroded his self-trust, the shattered self-trust magnified the perceived threat, and the intensified threat returned him to the triggers, each loop pulling him further from his old life. Finally, Rajesh sought help after missing three consecutive shifts and nearly colliding with a forklift while his mind raced with unanswerable questions. He came to the clinic exhausted, hoping to silence the internal alarm that had been ringing for years, though his deepest fear remained that seeking the truth of his captivity would shatter him completely and leave him entirely alone.
